rationale: A wins because it keeps the hard story inside the facts and knows when not to pitch past the proof. "Airtable just gave AI agents write access to enterprise data. What happens when one gets it wrong?" is the real uncomfortable editor question in this announcement. B has useful instincts, but "The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" turns one company update into market law, which is how decent strategy puts on a fake mustache and calls itself analysis.
gaps_in_A: "pre-AI decacorns rebrand to survive" is sharper than the fact set supports; the update gives valuation pressure, not evidence that Airtable is fighting for survival or that this is part of a proven decacorn pattern.
"formally retiring the \"spreadsheet-database\" identity" overstates "shifting its messaging"; retirement is a stronger corporate move than the supplied facts prove.
The valuation angle still needs a firmer monetization bridge; "any revenue or usage trajectory" is right, but without it this can become a vibes piece about an $11B company chasing AI heat.
gaps_in_B: "can an AI agent pivot close the gap from its peak?" implies a valuation-recovery thesis the update does not supply. Last valued at $11B and down from peak is not the same as proof this launch is meant to close that gap.

"The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market" universalizes from one Airtable announcement. That is a market trend only after parallel moves or analyst evidence, not before.
"Airtable just entered the AI agent market — that changes who it competes with" is plausible but underproved; no competitors, buyer comparisons, or analyst map appear in the update.

B spots reliability only in the question "what happens when an agent gets it wrong?" but fails to promote it into a real angle, even though undisclosed reliability data is one of the strongest facts in the brief.
